pos: n. (a large timber; rendering Greek dokos)
etymology: Old English beam, a tree or timber. Christ chose the largest structural member in a house for the thing a man cannot see in his own eye.
biblical_def: A beam is a large timber. Christ's image is deliberately absurd: “why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?… Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye” (Mat 7:3–5). Elisha's students go to Jordan to cut beams for a larger dwelling, and one borrowed axe head falls in (2Ki 6:2–5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beam as the largest, or a principal piece in a building, that lies across the walls; and a large piece of timber, long in proportion to its thickness.
webster_full: BEAM, n. The largest, or a principal piece in a building, that lies across the walls, and serves to support the principal rafters.
2. Any large piece of timber, long in proportion to its thickness.
3. The part of a balance from the ends of which the scales are suspended.
4. A ray of light.
scriptures: Mat 7:3
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Mat 7:5
Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.
Luk 6:41
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Let us go, we pray thee, unto Jordan, and take thence every man a beam, and let us make us a place there, where we may dwell. And he answered, Go ye.
corruption_summary: Correction is offered without self-examination, and Christ does not forbid removing the mote — He forbids doing it while carrying a beam.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:5 is routinely quoted as a prohibition on judging, and it is not. The sentence ends with an instruction: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye. The mote is real and is meant to come out. What is forbidden is attempting delicate eye surgery on someone else while a structural timber protrudes from one's own face.

The comedy of the image is the argument. A beam in the eye is physically impossible, and that is the point — the hypocrite's blindness to his own condition is as ridiculous as it is invisible to him. Christ calls him hypocrite, which in Greek meant an actor: a man performing the role of someone qualified to help.
roots_summary: Greek dokos (G1385), a beam of timber; karphos (G2595), a splinter or mote; hupokrites (G5273), an actor.
roots_lines: Greek dokos (G1385) — beam; Matthew 7:3-5, Luke 6:41-42.
Greek karphos (G2595) — mote, splinter; the same passages.
Greek hupokrites (G5273) — actor, hypocrite; Matthew 7:5.
usage: “Considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye” — invisible to its owner.
“First cast out the beam… and then shalt thou see clearly” — the mote still comes out.
“Thou hypocrite” — an actor playing someone qualified to help.

pos: adv. (with confident freedom; rendering Greek parrhesia)
etymology: From bold, Old English beald. The Greek parrhesia means all-speech — freedom to say everything, the right of a citizen rather than a slave.
biblical_def: Boldly means with confident freedom. Hebrews applies it to prayer: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16). Paul asks for prayer that he may “open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel” (Eph 6:19). The council marvels at Peter and John's boldness, “and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” (Act 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines boldly as in a bold manner; courageously; intrepidly; with confidence; and with excessive confidence, impudently.
webster_full: BOLDLY, adv. In a bold manner; courageously; intrepidly; without timidity or fear.
2. With excessive confidence; impudently.
scriptures: Heb 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
Eph 6:19
And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel,
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Act 4:31
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.
corruption_summary: Boldness is mistaken for temperament, and Acts traces it to company kept — they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:13 is one of the most encouraging verses for ordinary Christians: when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus. The council's explanation was not education, gifting, or personality. Something in the manner of two fishermen was traceable to whose company they had kept, and it was visible to hostile observers.

Hebrews 4:16 makes boldness the prescribed posture in prayer, and the grounding is in the previous verse: we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly. The confidence rests on the sympathy and sinlessness of the One at the throne, which means it is available on the worst day rather than only on the best.
roots_summary: Greek parrhesia (G3954), boldness, freedom of speech; parrhesiazomai (G3955), to speak boldly; tolmao (G5111), to dare.
roots_lines: Greek parrhesia (G3954) — boldness, confidence; Hebrews 4:16, 10:19, Acts 4:13, 29, 31.
Greek parrhesiazomai (G3955) — to speak boldly; Acts 9:27-29, 13:46, Ephesians 6:20.
Greek thronos charitos — throne of grace; Hebrews 4:16, the place boldness is exercised.
usage: “Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace” — grounded in the High Priest.
“That I may open my mouth boldly” — Paul asking for it in prison.
“They took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus” — the explanation given by enemies.

pos: v., n. (to obliterate; a blemish; rendering Hebrew machah, Greek exaleipho)
etymology: Middle English blotte, a stain. To blot out is to erase a record so completely that the writing cannot be recovered.
biblical_def: To blot is to erase. David prays, “blot out my transgressions… blot out all mine iniquities” (Psa 51:1,9). God promises, “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins” (Isa 43:25). Moses offers himself: “blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written” (Exo 32:32), and Christ promises the overcomer, “I will not blot out his name out of the book of life” (Rev 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blot as to spot with ink; to stain; to obliterate writing; to efface; to erase; and to blur, to disfigure.
webster_full: BLOT, v.t. To spot with ink; to stain or bespatter with ink.
2. To obliterate writing or letters; to efface; to erase; generally with out.
3. To efface; to erase; to cause to be forgotten; to destroy.
BLOT, n. A spot or stain on paper, usually applied to ink.
scriptures: Psa 51:1

To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin--; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written.
Rev 3:5
He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.
corruption_summary: Forgiveness is imagined as an overlooking, and Scripture's word is erasure — a record blotted out and deliberately not remembered.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 43:25 states both halves and names the motive: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins. The blotting is God's own act, done for His own sake rather than for any merit found in the offender, and it is followed by a decision not to remember. Divine forgetting is not a failure of memory; it is a judicial commitment never to raise the matter again.

Exodus 32:32 is one of the great intercessory sentences in Scripture. After the golden calf, Moses offers, yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin—; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written. The sentence breaks off unfinished, and he offers his own erasure in exchange. Paul echoes it in Romans 9, and both point toward One who actually did make the exchange.
roots_summary: Hebrew machah (H4229), to wipe, blot out; Greek exaleipho (G1813), to wipe away, erase — the same verb as wiping tears.
roots_lines: Hebrew machah (H4229) — to blot out, wipe; Psalm 51:1, 9, Isaiah 43:25, Exodus 32:32-33.
Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to blot out, wipe away; Acts 3:19, Colossians 2:14, Revelation 3:5.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — book, scroll; the book Moses asked to be blotted from.
usage: “Blot out my transgressions” — erasure, not overlooking.
“Will not remember thy sins” — a commitment, not a lapse.
“Blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book” — Moses offering the exchange.

pos: v. (to surround, hem in; rendering Hebrew sabab, Greek euperistatos)
etymology: From be- and set — to set about on all sides. To be beset is to be surrounded, not merely troubled.
biblical_def: To be beset is to be surrounded. The psalmist says of God's knowledge, “Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me” (Psa 139:5). Hebrews names “the sin which doth so easily beset us” and commands laying it aside along with every weight (Heb 12:1). The men of Gibeah beset the house round about (Jdg 19:22; 20:5), and the psalmist elsewhere says the wicked have beset him about (Psa 22:12 in the surrounding imagery).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beset as to surround; to inclose; to hem in; to besiege; to press on all sides, so as to perplex; and to embarrass.
webster_full: BESET, v.t. To surround; to inclose; to hem in; to besiege; as, we are beset with enemies.
2. To press on all sides, so as to perplex; to entangle, so as to render escape difficult or impossible.
3. To waylay.
4. To fall upon.
scriptures: Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,

Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door, and spake to the master of the house, the old man, saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
corruption_summary: Besetting sin is treated as an identity to be managed, and Hebrews puts it in a sentence about laying things aside before a race.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:1 distinguishes two things a runner drops: let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us. A weight is not sinful — it is simply anything that slows a runner, and much of what Christians carry is in that category. The besetting sin is the second item, and the instruction for both is identical and unsentimental: lay it aside. Not analyse, not accommodate.

Psalm 139:5 uses the same word for something entirely different: thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me. Being surrounded by God is presented as inescapable and, in the psalm's development, as comfort rather than threat — whither shall I flee from thy presence? The same verb describes a hostile encirclement in Judges and a sheltering one here.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsur (H6696) and sabab (H5437), to surround, encircle; Greek euperistatos (G2139), easily surrounding — used only in Hebrews 12:1.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsur (H6696) — to besiege, beset; Psalm 139:5.
Hebrew sabab (H5437) — to surround, encompass; Judges 19:22, 20:5.
Greek euperistatos (G2139) — easily besetting; only Hebrews 12:1.
usage: “Thou hast beset me behind and before” — encirclement as comfort.
“The sin which doth so easily beset us” — laid aside, not managed.
“Lay aside every weight” — and much of it is not sin at all.

pos: v. (to give, to store; rendering Greek didomi and sunago)
etymology: From be- and stow, a place — to put in a place. To bestow is to place something with someone, whether as gift or storage.
biblical_def: To bestow is to give or to store. The rich fool asks, “What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?” and answers himself by building greater barns (Luk 12:17–18). John marvels, “Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God” (1Jn 3:1). Paul says he bestowed much labour on the Galatians (Gal 4:11) and warns that giving all his goods to feed the poor without charity profits nothing (1Co 13:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bestow as to give; to confer; to impart; with the sense of gratuity; to give in marriage; and to lay up in store, to deposit for safe keeping.
webster_full: BESTOW, v.t. To give; to confer; to impart; with the sense of gratuity, and followed by on or upon.
2. To give in marriage; to dispose of.
3. To apply; to place for the purpose of exertion, or use.
4. To lay up in store; to deposit for safe keeping; to stow; to place.
scriptures: And he thought within himself, saying, What shall I do, because I have no room where to bestow my fruits?
Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God: therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not.
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater; and there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods.
corruption_summary: Storage is treated as prudence and giving as generosity, and Luke's rich fool is condemned not for wealth but for a soliloquy in which every pronoun is his own.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 12:17-19 is worth reading for its grammar: what shall I do… I will pull down my barns… there will I bestow all my fruits and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up. Eleven first-person pronouns in three verses, and no other person appears in the plan — no neighbour, no poor, no God. God's response addresses the missing party: Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee.

1 John 3:1 uses the same verb for the opposite motion: behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God. The word manner carries the sense of what foreign kind — love of an unfamiliar sort. The contrast with the barn-builder is complete: one man storing his own goods for himself, and a Father placing an unearned name on strangers.
roots_summary: Greek sunago (G4863), to gather, bestow in storage; didomi (G1325), to give; psomizo (G5595), to feed out in morsels, in 1 Corinthians 13:3.
roots_lines: Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together, bestow; Luke 12:17-18.
Greek didomi (G1325) — to give, bestow; 1 John 3:1.
Greek potapos (G4217) — of what kind, what manner; 1 John 3:1, love of a foreign sort.
usage: “No room where to bestow my fruits” — a plan with no other person in it.
“What manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us” — love of an unfamiliar kind.
“Though I bestow all my goods… and have not charity” — giving without love profits nothing.

pos: adj. (without floor; rendering Greek abussos)
etymology: Bottom with the privative ending. The Greek abussos gives us abyss — a depth with no measurable floor.
biblical_def: Bottomless describes the abyss. Revelation gives it a key and a keeper: “there was given unto him the key of the bottomless pit” (Rev 9:1), and later an angel comes down “having the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand” to bind the dragon (Rev 20:1–3). The beast ascends out of it (Rev 11:7), and Paul uses the same word of the deep: “Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead)” (Rom 10:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bottomless as without a bottom; having no bottom; fathomless.
webster_full: BOTTOMLESS, a. Without a bottom; having no bottom; fathomless.
scriptures: Rev 9:1
And the fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star fall from heaven unto the earth: and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit.
Rev 20:1
And I saw an angel come down from heaven, having the key of the bottomless pit and a great chain in his hand.
Rev 11:7
And when they shall have finished their testimony, the beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them.
Rom 10:7
Or, Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.)
corruption_summary: Evil is imagined as either mythological or merely psychological, and Revelation describes a place with a key — held, and not by the powers inside it.
corruption_paragraphs: The recurring detail in Revelation is the key. The bottomless pit is never described as open by its own power; something is given a key, or an angel comes down having the key and a great chain. Whatever is in the abyss is contained, and the containment is administered from outside. That single structural fact governs how a Christian should read every account of evil's activity in history.

Revelation 20:1-3 presses it further: the angel laid hold on the dragon… and bound him a thousand years, and cast him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a seal upon him. Four verbs of restraint in one sentence. The abyss is bottomless from the inside; from above it has a lid, a lock, and a seal.
roots_summary: Greek abussos (G12), bottomless, the abyss — also the Septuagint's word for the deep of Genesis 1:2.
roots_lines: Greek abussos (G12) — bottomless pit, abyss; Revelation 9:1-11, 11:7, 17:8, 20:1-3, Luke 8:31.
Greek kleis (G2807) — key; Revelation 9:1, 20:1, and 1:18, I have the keys of hell and of death.
Greek halusis (G254) — chain; Revelation 20:1.
usage: “The key of the bottomless pit” — held, and not from inside.
“Bound him… shut him up, and set a seal upon him” — four verbs of restraint.
“Who shall descend into the deep?” — Paul's rhetorical impossibility.

pos: n. (a foreigner of another tongue; rendering Greek barbaros)
etymology: From Greek barbaros, imitative of unintelligible speech — bar-bar. A barbarian is simply someone whose language you cannot understand.
biblical_def: A barbarian is a foreigner of another tongue. Paul uses it without contempt: “if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me” (1Co 14:11) — the term is mutual and depends only on comprehension. He declares himself “debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians” (Rom 1:14), and Colossians abolishes the category in Christ: “there is neither Greek nor Jew… Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all” (Col 3:11). Luke calls the Maltese barbarous people who showed no little kindness (Act 28:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines barbarian as a man in his rude, savage state; an uncivilized person; a foreigner; and among the Greeks and Romans, a foreigner, one who did not speak their language.
webster_full: BARBARIAN, n. A man in his rude, savage state; an uncivilized person.
2. A cruel, savage, brutal man; one destitute of pity or humanity.
3. A foreigner. The Greeks and Romans denominated most foreign nations barbarians.
scriptures: Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Rom 1:14
I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise.
Col 3:11
Where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free: but Christ is all, and in all.
Act 28:2
And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
corruption_summary: Cultural distance is read as inferiority, and Paul makes barbarian a purely mutual term — whoever cannot understand you is your barbarian too.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:11 removes any hierarchy from the word: I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me. The label attaches symmetrically. Whatever superiority a Greek felt in using it was an accident of which language happened to be his own, and Paul makes the point while arguing that unintelligible speech in the assembly helps no one.

Acts 28:2 supplies the practical refutation. Shipwrecked, cold, and soaked, Luke writes: and the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold. The people the Greek word dismissed were the ones who lit the fire. Colossians finishes the argument by naming the category and abolishing it — Barbarian, Scythian… but Christ is all, and in all.
roots_summary: Greek barbaros (G915), a non-Greek speaker, foreigner; the term is phonetic mockery of unintelligible speech rather than a moral judgment.
roots_lines: Greek barbaros (G915) — barbarian, foreigner; 1 Corinthians 14:11, Romans 1:14, Colossians 3:11, Acts 28:2, 4.
Greek Skuthes (G4658) — Scythian; Colossians 3:11, the byword for the most remote barbarian.
Greek philanthropia (G5363) — kindness; Acts 28:2, the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness.
usage: “He that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me” — the label attaches both ways.
“Debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians” — the gospel owed to both.
“The barbarous people shewed us no little kindness” — they lit the fire.

pos: v. (to gather together; rendering Hebrew qahal, Greek sunago)
etymology: From Latin ad and simul, together. To assemble is to bring into one place — and the Hebrew root gives Israel its word for congregation.
biblical_def: To assemble is to gather. Solomon assembles the elders for the temple dedication (1Ki 8:1). Nehemiah's reforms begin when the people assemble with fasting (Neh 9:1). The prophets promise regathering: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel” (Mic 2:12), and Zephaniah says God's determination is “to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them mine indignation” (Zep 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assemble as to collect a number of individuals or particulars into one place or body; to bring or call together; to convene; to congregate.
webster_full: ASSEMBLE, v.t. To collect a number of individuals or particulars into one place, or body; to bring or call together; to convene; to congregate.
ASSEMBLE, v.i. To meet or come together; to convene, as a number of individuals.
scriptures: Mic 2:12

I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.
Neh 9:1
Now in the twenty and fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackclothes, and earth upon them.

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, and all the heads of the tribes, the chief of the fathers of the children of Israel, unto king Solomon in Jerusalem, that they might bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.
Zep 3:8

Therefore wait ye upon me, saith the LORD, until the day that I rise up to the prey: for my determination is to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms, to pour upon them mine indignation, even all my fierce anger: for all the earth shall be devoured with the fire of my jealousy.
corruption_summary: Gathering is treated as one means among many, and the Hebrew word for congregation is built from the verb — Israel is defined by being assembled.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 2:12 doubles the verbs for certainty: I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah. Scattering was the judgment; assembling is the promise. That pattern runs from Babel to Pentecost, where men of every nation heard in their own tongues, and it makes any voluntary scattering of God's people a strange thing for them to choose.

Nehemiah 9:1 shows what an assembly is for: now in the twenty and fourth day of this month the children of Israel were assembled with fasting, and with sackclothes, and earth upon them. They stood and read in the book of the law one fourth part of the day, and another fourth part they confessed. Gathering, Scripture, and confession occupying the same hours — which is a fair description of what an assembly was understood to be.
roots_summary: Hebrew qahal (H6950), to assemble — the root of qahal, congregation, rendered ekklesia in the Septuagint; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather.
roots_lines: Hebrew qahal (H6950) — to assemble, convoke; 1 Kings 8:1, Numbers 20:8.
Hebrew qahal (H6951) — congregation, assembly; the Septuagint renders it ekklesia, church.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — assembling together; Hebrews 10:25, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves.
usage: “I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee” — scattering judged, gathering promised.
“Assembled with fasting… and read in the book of the law” — what an assembly was for.
“That I may assemble the kingdoms” — the nations gathered for judgment.

pos: adj. (heedful, listening closely; rendering Hebrew qashab)
etymology: From Latin attendere, to stretch toward. Attention is a stretching of the mind toward something — effortful rather than passive.
biblical_def: Attentive means listening closely. Nehemiah asks God, “let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant” (Neh 1:6). Ezra's reading is received the same way: “the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law” (Neh 8:3). Solomon's dedication prayer asks that God's ears be attent unto the prayer made in this place (2Ch 6:40), and Luke says the people “were very attentive to hear him” (Luk 19:48).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines attentive as heedful; intent; observant; regarding with care.
webster_full: ATTENTIVE, a. Heedful; intent; observant; regarding with care.
ATTENTION, n. The act of attending or heeding; the due application of the ear to sounds, or of the mind to objects presented to its contemplation.
scriptures: Neh 1:6

Let thine ear now be attentive, and thine eyes open, that thou mayest hear the prayer of thy servant, which I pray before thee now, day and night, for the children of Israel thy servants, and confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against thee: both I and my father's house have sinned.
Neh 8:3

And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law.
Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place.
And could not find what they might do: for all the people were very attentive to hear him.
corruption_summary: Distraction is treated as a personal failing to be willed away, and Scripture treats attention as the thing a whole congregation gives or withholds together.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 8:3 records a scene almost impossible to imagine now: he read therein… from the morning until midday… and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law. Hours of public Scripture reading, and the detail the chronicler thought worth preserving is the quality of the listening. Attention is described as a corporate act — the ears of all the people — not a private discipline each person managed alone.

Luke 19:48 shows attention as protection: the chief priests and the scribes sought to destroy him, and could not find what they might do: for all the people were very attentive to hear him. A listening crowd was the only thing preventing an arrest. Genuine attention to the word of God has political consequences, which is why it has always been the first thing an opposing power tries to break up.
roots_summary: Hebrew qashab (H7181), to prick up the ear, attend; ozen qashshubah, an attentive ear; Greek ekkremamai (G1582), to hang upon, in Luke 19:48.
roots_lines: Hebrew qashab (H7181) — to attend, listen; Nehemiah 1:6, 11, 2 Chronicles 6:40, 7:15.
Hebrew ozen (H241) — ear; the attentive ear of Nehemiah's prayer.
Greek ekkremamai (G1582) — to hang upon; only Luke 19:48, very attentive to hear him.
usage: “Let thine ear now be attentive” — asked of God in prayer.
“The ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law” — a corporate act.
“All the people were very attentive to hear him” — and it prevented an arrest.

pos: v. (to make beautiful; rendering Hebrew paar)
etymology: From beauty, Latin bellus. To beautify is to adorn a thing to its proper glory rather than to disguise it.
biblical_def: To beautify is to make beautiful. Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to “beautify the house of the LORD which is in Jerusalem” (Ezr 7:27). Isaiah promises timber brought “to beautify the place of my sanctuary” (Isa 60:13). And the psalmist turns the verb on people: “the LORD taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation” (Psa 149:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beautify as to make or render beautiful; to adorn; to deck; to grace; to add beauty to; to embellish.
webster_full: BEAUTIFY, v.t. To make or render beautiful; to adorn; to deck; to grace; to add beauty to; to embellish.
BEAUTIFY, v.i. To become beautiful; to advance in beauty.
scriptures: For the LORD taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation.
Ezr 7:27
Blessed be the LORD God of our fathers, which hath put such a thing as this in the king's heart, to beautify the house of the LORD which is in Jerusalem:
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
corruption_summary: Beauty is pursued as self-improvement, and Psalm 149 says God beautifies the meek — the trait least associated with attractiveness.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 149:4 pairs two things that rarely appear together: the LORD taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation. The beautifying agent is salvation, and the recipients are the meek. Every culture beautifies the assertive and the accomplished; this promise runs to the people at the back. It is also stated as future — he will beautify — which means present plainness is not the final assessment.

Isaiah 61:3 uses the same instinct in its most quoted form: to appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. Three exchanges, each giving the mourner something better than what was taken. The chapter Christ read in Nazareth contains this promise two verses past where He stopped.
roots_summary: Hebrew paar (H6286), to glorify, beautify; tiphereth (H8597), beauty, glory; peer (H6287), a headdress or ornament.
roots_lines: Hebrew paar (H6286) — to beautify, glorify; Psalm 149:4, Ezra 7:27, Isaiah 60:7, 13.
Hebrew tiphereth (H8597) — beauty, glory; Isaiah 60:19, 61:3.
Hebrew peer (H6287) — ornament, garland; Isaiah 61:3, beauty for ashes.
usage: “He will beautify the meek with salvation” — the promise runs to the back of the room.
“To beautify the house of the LORD” — a pagan king's commission.
“Beauty for ashes” — three exchanges, each an upgrade.

pos: v. (looked upon with attention; rendering Greek theaomai)
etymology: Past tense of behold, from be- and hold — to hold with the eyes. Beholding is sustained looking rather than a glance.
biblical_def: To have beheld is to have looked with attention. John's prologue rests a claim on it: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (Joh 1:14). Christ says, “I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven” (Luk 10:18). At the crucifixion the people “beheld the things which were done” and smote their breasts (Luk 23:48), and at the ascension the disciples “beheld, he was taken up” (Act 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines behold as to fix the eyes upon; to see with attention; to observe with care; and as an imperative, look, see, observe.
webster_full: BEHOLD, v.t. To fix the eyes upon; to see with attention; to observe with care.
BEHOLD, v.i. To look; to direct the eyes to an object.
2. To fix the attention upon an object; to attend; to direct or fix the mind.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
And he said unto them, I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.
Act 1:9
And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.
And all the people that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were done, smote their breasts, and returned.
corruption_summary: Christian claims are defended as reasonable inferences, and the apostles kept resting them on something cruder — we beheld.
corruption_paragraphs: John 1:14 makes an eyewitness claim in the middle of the most theological paragraph in the New Testament: and we beheld his glory. The same writer opens his first epistle the same way — that which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled. The doctrine of the incarnation is presented as testimony about something watched at close range, which is a strange way to advance a myth and the ordinary way to report an event.

Luke 23:48 records a different beholding and its effect: all the people that came together to that sight, beholding the things which were done, smote their breasts, and returned. A crowd that had come to watch an execution went home striking themselves. Luke does not say they believed; he says what they did with their hands, which is often the more honest report.
roots_summary: Greek theaomai (G2300), to gaze upon, behold — the root of theatre; theoreo (G2334), to observe attentively.
roots_lines: Greek theaomai (G2300) — to behold, gaze; John 1:14, 1 John 1:1.
Greek theoreo (G2334) — to look at, observe; Luke 10:18, 23:48, Acts 1:11.
Greek skenoo (G4637) — to tabernacle, dwell; John 1:14, dwelt among us.
usage: “We beheld his glory” — an eyewitness claim inside a theological prologue.
“I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven” — reported by One who watched.
“Beholding the things which were done, smote their breasts” — what the crowd did with its hands.

pos: v. (to shun, keep away from; rendering Greek ekklino and periistemi)
etymology: From Old French esvuidier, to empty out. To avoid is to make oneself absent from something.
biblical_def: To avoid is to shun. Paul commands it of divisive people: “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17). Of empty controversy: “shun profane and vain babblings… but foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes” (2Ti 2:16,23). Proverbs says of the wicked path, “Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away” (Pro 4:15), and Paul avoids blame in handling money (2Co 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines avoid as to shun; to keep at a distance from; to endeavor to escape; to evade; and to quit, to evacuate.
webster_full: AVOID, v.t. To shun; to keep at a distance from; that is, literally, to go or be wide from.
2. To shift off, or clear off; as, to avoid expense.
3. To quit; to evacuate; to shun by leaving.
4. To escape; as, to avoid danger.
scriptures: Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.
Pro 4:15
Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away.
Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us:
corruption_summary: Endless engagement is treated as a virtue, and Paul repeatedly commands avoidance — of divisive people, of questions that only generate strife, and of any handling of money that invites suspicion.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 4:15 uses four verbs for one instruction: avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away. The repetition is not padding. It addresses the way temptation is usually approached — not entered deliberately but drifted toward, walked past, glanced at, and finally joined. Each verb closes a stage, and the last one requires actual movement in the opposite direction.

2 Timothy 2:23 gives the pastoral criterion: foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes. The test is not whether the question is interesting but what it reliably produces. Some disputes are worth having; some are known in advance to yield nothing but heat, and a minister who cannot tell them apart will spend his ministry on the second kind.
roots_summary: Greek ekklino (G1578), to turn away, avoid; periistemi (G4026), to stand around, shun; paraiteomai (G3868), to decline.
roots_lines: Greek ekklino (G1578) — to turn aside, avoid; Romans 16:17, 1 Peter 3:11, let him eschew evil.
Greek periistemi (G4026) — to shun, avoid; 2 Timothy 2:16, Titus 3:9.
Greek paraiteomai (G3868) — to refuse, avoid; 2 Timothy 2:23, 1 Timothy 4:7.
usage: “Mark them which cause divisions… and avoid them” — identification, then distance.
“Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it” — four verbs closing four stages.
“Avoiding this, that no man should blame us” — suspicion forestalled in money.

pos: v., adj. (made certain; rendering Greek pistoo and plerophoreo)
etymology: From Latin ad and securus, safe. To be assured is to be made certain — the certainty coming from outside the one assured.
biblical_def: To be assured is to be made certain. Paul charges Timothy, “continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them” (2Ti 3:14). John says, “hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him” (1Jn 3:19). Isaiah promises that “the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assure as to make certain; to give confidence by a promise; to declare positively to; to confirm; and to make secure with respect to a future event.
webster_full: ASSURE, v.t. To make certain; to give confidence by a promise, declaration, or other evidence.
2. To confirm; to make certain or secure.
3. To embolden; to make confident.
4. To make secure, with of before the object secured.
scriptures: But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them;
And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.
Col 2:2

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ;
corruption_summary: Assurance is sought in the strength of one's feelings, and 2 Timothy grounds it in who taught you and 1 John in what you actually do.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Timothy 3:14 gives an unusual ground for confidence: continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them. The assurance rests partly on the credibility of the teachers — in Timothy's case a grandmother, a mother, and Paul. That is not a substitute for personal conviction, but it is a real support, and it means a believer's confidence is not required to be manufactured from nothing.

1 John 3:18-19 supplies the other ground, and it is behavioural: let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth. And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him. A heart that accuses its owner is quieted by evidence of real love shown in action — and John adds the sentence that saves this from becoming a new anxiety: if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart.
roots_summary: Greek pistoo (G4104), to make faithful, assure; plerophoria (G4136), full assurance; peitho (G3982), to persuade.
roots_lines: Greek pistoo (G4104) — to assure, be confirmed; only 2 Timothy 3:14.
Greek plerophoria (G4136) — full assurance; Colossians 2:2, Hebrews 6:11, 10:22.
Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade, assure; 1 John 3:19.
usage: “Knowing of whom thou hast learned them” — assurance partly resting on the teachers.
“Shall assure our hearts before him” — quieted by evidence of real love.
“Quietness and assurance for ever” — righteousness' long effect.

pos: n. (a hearing, those hearing; rendering Hebrew ozen, Greek akoe)
etymology: From Latin audire, to hear. In the KJV audience means the act of hearing as much as the people doing it — to speak in the audience of the people is to speak in their hearing.
biblical_def: An audience is a hearing. Abraham buys Machpelah publicly, “in the audience of the sons of Heth” (Gen 23:13). Moses reads the book of the covenant “in the audience of the people” (Exo 24:7). Christ finishes His sayings “in the audience of the people” (Luk 7:1), and Paul's defence in Acts turns on whether the crowd will give him audience (Act 13:16; 22:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines audience as the act of hearing, or attending to sounds; admittance to a hearing; and an auditory, an assembly of hearers.
webster_full: AUDIENCE, n. The act of hearing, or attending to sounds.
2. Admittance to a hearing; public reception to an interview.
3. An auditory; an assembly of hearers.
4. In the Spanish dominions, a court of judicature.
scriptures: And he spake unto Ephron in the audience of the people of the land, saying, But if thou wilt give it, I pray thee, hear me: I will give thee money for the field; take it of me, and I will bury my dead there.
Exo 24:7
And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.
Luk 7:1
Now when he had ended all his sayings in the audience of the people, he entered into Capernaum.
And they gave him audience unto this word, and then lifted up their voices, and said, Away with such a fellow from the earth: for it is not fit that he should live.
corruption_summary: Transactions and vows are made privately and disputed later, and Scripture keeps staging them in the audience of witnesses who could contradict them.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 23 is a property transaction conducted with deliberate publicity: Abraham speaks in the audience of the people of the land, weighs four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant, and the field is made sure unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth. He could have accepted it as a gift and did not, precisely so that no one could later question the title. Public witness is cheap at the time and priceless afterward.

Exodus 24:7 is the covenant's own model: he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient. The terms were read aloud before the agreement was made, which is the opposite of how most commitments are entered. A congregation that hears the terms plainly before consenting is following Sinai's procedure.
roots_summary: Hebrew ozen (H241), ear — the idiom in the ears of; Greek akoe (G189), hearing; akouo (G191), to hear.
roots_lines: Hebrew ozen (H241) — ear; Genesis 23:13, 16, Exodus 24:7, in the audience of.
Greek akoe (G189) — hearing, audience; Luke 7:1, Acts 17:20.
Greek akouo (G191) — to hear, give audience; Acts 13:16, 15:12, 22:22.
usage: “In the audience of the sons of Heth” — a purchase made unquestionable.
“Read in the audience of the people” — terms heard before consent.
“They gave him audience unto this word” — and then the crowd turned.

pos: v. (signalled by a gesture; rendering Greek kataneuo and kataseio)
etymology: From Old English beacnian, to make a sign — related to beacon. A beckon is communication without words.
biblical_def: To beckon is to signal by gesture. Peter and John's partners are beckoned to bring the second ship when the nets break (Luk 5:7). Zacharias, struck dumb in the temple, “beckoned unto them, and remained speechless” (Luk 1:22). Peter, released from prison, “beckoning unto them with the hand to hold their peace, declared unto them how the Lord had brought him out” (Act 12:17), and Paul beckons with the hand before speaking to a crowd (Act 13:16; 21:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beckon as to make a sign to another, by nodding, winking, or a motion of the hand or finger, intended as a hint or intimation.
webster_full: BECKON, v.i. To make a sign to another, by nodding, winking, or a motion of the hand or finger, etc., intended as a hint or intimation.
BECKON, v.t. To make a significant sign to.
scriptures: Luk 5:7
And they beckoned unto their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they began to sink.
Luk 1:22
And when he came out, he could not speak unto them: and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple: for he beckoned unto them, and remained speechless.

But he, beckoning unto them with the hand to hold their peace, declared unto them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, Go shew these things unto James, and to the brethren. And he departed, and went into another place.
And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,
corruption_summary: Help is declined out of pride, and Luke's fishermen beckoned for a second boat the moment their own nets broke.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 5:6-7 records a small and telling detail: they inclosed a great multitude of fishes: and their net brake. And they beckoned unto their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. The catch was too large for one crew, and their first instinct was to signal for help rather than to lose the fish protecting their own achievement. Both ships filled, and both began to sink.

Zacharias' beckoning is the opposite situation — a priest who came out of the temple unable to pronounce the blessing the people were waiting for, and could only gesture. He had asked for a sign and received one: nine months of silence. Luke notes he remained speechless, and the first words recorded from him afterward are a song.
roots_summary: Greek kataneuo (G2656), to nod, beckon; kataseio (G2678), to shake down, beckon with the hand; dianeuo (G1269), to signal, in Luke 1:22.
roots_lines: Greek kataneuo (G2656) — to beckon, nod; only Luke 5:7.
Greek kataseio (G2678) — to beckon with the hand; Acts 12:17, 13:16, 19:33, 21:40.
Greek dianeuo (G1269) — to make signs; only Luke 1:22.
usage: “They beckoned unto their partners… that they should come and help them” — help signalled at once.
“He beckoned unto them, and remained speechless” — a priest who could not bless.
“Beckoning unto them with the hand to hold their peace” — Peter at the door.

pos: v. (to conduct oneself; rendering Hebrew sakal, Greek anastrepho)
etymology: From be- and have, in the older sense of to hold or bear oneself. Behaviour is how a person carries himself, and Scripture ties it to place and office.
biblical_def: To behave is to conduct oneself. Paul tells Timothy the purpose of his letter: “that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). Charity “doth not behave itself unseemly” (1Co 13:5). David behaved himself wisely (1Sa 18:14), and the psalmist resolves, “I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way” (Psa 101:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines behave as to restrain; to govern; to subdue; and to carry, to conduct, used with the reciprocal pronoun, as to behave one's self.
webster_full: BEHAVE, v.t. To restrain; to govern; to subdue.
2. To carry; to conduct; used with the reciprocal pronoun; as, he behaves himself manfully.
BEHAVIOR, n. Manner of behaving, whether good or bad; conduct; manners; carriage of one's self.
scriptures: But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
And David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
corruption_summary: Church conduct is treated as a matter of preference, and Paul wrote a whole letter so that Timothy would know how men ought to behave in God's house.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 3:15 states the letter's purpose and grounds it in what a church is: that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. Behaviour follows from identity. If the assembly is merely a voluntary society, conduct within it is a matter of taste; if it is the household of the living God and the pillar of the truth, conduct is a matter of fitness.

1 Corinthians 13:5 supplies the shortest test: charity doth not behave itself unseemly. Love has manners. That is not a trivial claim in a chapter about the greatest of the graces — it means that rudeness in the name of honesty, or roughness in the name of zeal, has failed a criterion the apostle thought worth listing beside not seeking her own and thinking no evil.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal (H7919), to act prudently; Greek anastrepho (G390), to conduct oneself; aschemoneo (G807), to behave unseemly.
roots_lines: Greek anastrepho (G390) — to behave, conduct oneself; 1 Timothy 3:15, 2 Corinthians 1:12.
Greek aschemoneo (G807) — to behave unbecomingly; 1 Corinthians 13:5, 7:36.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to behave wisely, prosper; 1 Samuel 18:14-15, Psalm 101:2.
usage: “How thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God” — conduct following identity.
“Doth not behave itself unseemly” — love has manners.
“I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way” — tested inside the house.

pos: n. (plunder taken in war; rendering Hebrew baz and malqoach)
etymology: From Old Norse byti, exchange or share. Booty is captured goods divided among captors — and Scripture regulates the division carefully.
biblical_def: Booty is plunder. Moses divides the Midianite spoil between those who went to battle and the whole congregation, with a tribute levied for the LORD (Num 31:27,32). Jeremiah promises the faithful Ethiopian Ebedmelech, “thy life shall be for a prey unto thee” (Jer 39:18). Habakkuk asks whether the Chaldean shall “empty his net, and not spare continually to slay the nations” (Hab 1:17), and Zephaniah says the remnant shall take the booty of the proud (Zep 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines booty as spoil taken from an enemy in war; plunder; pillage; and that which is seized by violence and robbery.
webster_full: BOOTY, n. Spoil taken from an enemy in war; plunder; pillage.
2. That which is seized by violence and robbery.
scriptures: And divide the prey into two parts; between them that took the war upon them, who went out to battle, and between all the congregation:
For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.
Zep 2:9

Therefore as I live, saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, even the breeding of nettles, and saltpits, and a perpetual desolation: the residue of my people shall spoil them, and the remnant of my people shall possess them.
Hab 1:17
Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?
corruption_summary: Reward is claimed by whoever did the visible work, and Israel's spoil law divided it between the men who fought and the congregation who stayed.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 31:27 legislates a division that soldiers would not have chosen: divide the prey into two parts; between them that took the war upon them, who went out to battle, and between all the congregation. The men who risked their lives received half; the people who stayed home received the other half. David later makes the same ruling permanent after Ziklag — as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff.

The principle protects a community from being sorted into heroes and dependants. Those who go and those who hold the ground both share, because the enterprise belonged to all of them. Applied to a church, it means the visible worker and the quiet supporter are on the same ledger, which is roughly what Paul says about the body's less honourable members receiving more abundant honour.
roots_summary: Hebrew baz (H957), spoil, booty; malqoach (H4455), prey taken; shalal (H7998), spoil.
roots_lines: Hebrew malqoach (H4455) — booty, prey; Numbers 31:11-12, 26-27, 32.
Hebrew baz (H957) — spoil, booty; Zephaniah 2:9, Isaiah 10:6.
Hebrew shalal (H7998) — spoil, prey; Jeremiah 39:18, thy life shall be for a prey.
usage: “Divide the prey… between them that took the war… and… all the congregation” — a division soldiers would not have chosen.
“Thy life shall be for a prey unto thee” — the reward promised to a faithful foreigner.
“The residue of my people shall… possess them” — Zephaniah's reversal.

pos: n. (the edge of a river or pit; rendering Hebrew saphah)
etymology: Middle English brink, an edge. The brink is the last solid ground before water — and Scripture stations several people there.
biblical_def: A brink is an edge. Moses' mother lays the ark “in the flags by the river's brink” (Exo 2:3), and Pharaoh's daughter finds it there. Moses is told to stand by the river's brink with the rod that turned to a serpent (Exo 7:15). Pharaoh's dream kine come up “and fed in a meadow” by the river's brink (Gen 41:3), and Ezekiel's man with the line brings him back “to the brink of the river” where trees grow on both sides (Eze 47:6–7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brink as the edge, margin or border of a steep place, as of a precipice, or the bank of a river.
webster_full: BRINK, n. The edge, margin or border of a steep place, as of a precipice, or the bank of a river.
scriptures: Exo 2:3
And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink.
Exo 7:15

Get thee unto Pharaoh in the morning; lo, he goeth out unto the water; and thou shalt stand by the river's brink against he come; and the rod which was turned to a serpent shalt thou take in thine hand.
Eze 47:6
And he said unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen this? Then he brought me, and caused me to return to the brink of the river.
Gen 41:3
And, behold, seven other kine came up after them out of the river, ill favoured and leanfleshed; and stood by the other kine upon the brink of the river.
corruption_summary: Desperate action is read as a failure of faith, and Moses' mother put her son in a basket at the water's edge because it was the only thing left to do.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 2:3 describes an act with no guarantees: when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river's brink. She waterproofed it carefully and then let it go. Hebrews 11 calls this faith and notes the parents were not afraid of the king's commandment. Faith here looks exactly like a mother doing the last thing available to her.

Ezekiel 47's brink is a place of measurement and then of trees. The prophet is led out into water to the ankles, the knees, the loins, and finally waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over — and then brought back to the brink to see what grows along it. The vantage point from the edge is where the growth becomes visible.
roots_summary: Hebrew saphah (H8193), lip, edge, brink — the same word for a human lip and a river's margin.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphah (H8193) — lip, edge, brink; Exodus 2:3, 7:15, Genesis 41:3, Ezekiel 47:6.
Hebrew tebah (H8392) — ark, chest; Exodus 2:3, the same word as Noah's ark.
Hebrew gome (H1573) — bulrush, papyrus; the ark's material.
usage: “She laid it in the flags by the river's brink” — the last thing available, called faith.
“Stand by the river's brink against he come” — Moses posted with the rod.
“Brought me, and caused me to return to the brink” — where the trees are seen.

pos: adj. (confident, daring; rendering Greek tolmao and parrhesia)
etymology: Old English beald, brave. Boldness in Scripture is a property of the righteous and a request of the timid.
biblical_def: Bold means confident. Proverbs contrasts two conditions: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1). Paul says he was “bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention” (1Th 2:2), having been shamefully entreated at Philippi. He tells the Corinthians he is not bold in presence but bold in letters (2Co 10:1), and Isaiah records God saying, “I was found of them that sought me not… I said, Behold me, behold me” (Isa 65:1, quoted in Rom 10:20 as Isaiah being very bold).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bold as daring; courageous; brave; intrepid; fearless; and requiring courage in the execution; also, executed with spirit or loftiness.
webster_full: BOLD, a. Daring; courageous; brave; intrepid; fearless; applied to men or other animals.
2. Requiring courage in the execution; executed with spirit or boldness; planned with courage and spirit.
3. Confident; not timorous.
4. In an ill sense, rude, forward, impudent.
scriptures: Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention.
But Esaias is very bold, and saith, I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me.
Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you:
corruption_summary: Boldness is assumed to come from a clear conscience alone, and Proverbs makes it the fruit of righteousness while cowardice is the fruit of guilt.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 28:1 states a causal relationship most people feel before they can explain it: the wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. Guilt manufactures pursuers that do not exist. A man carrying something unconfessed reads ordinary events as closing in, and no amount of reassurance settles him, because the pursuit is internal. Righteousness produces boldness the same way — not by bravado, but by removing the reason to look over one's shoulder.

1 Thessalonians 2:2 shows boldness surviving its own cost: even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention. He had been beaten and jailed in the previous city and preached in the next one anyway. The phrase bold in our God locates the source, which is why the beating did not settle the question.
roots_summary: Greek tolmao (G5111), to dare; parrhesiazomai (G3955), to speak boldly; apotolmao (G662), to be very bold, in Romans 10:20.
roots_lines: Greek parrhesiazomai (G3955) — to be bold in speech; 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Acts 9:27.
Greek apotolmao (G662) — to be very bold; only Romans 10:20, of Isaiah.
Greek tharreo (G2292) — to be confident, bold; 2 Corinthians 10:1-2.
usage: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth” — guilt manufactures pursuers.
“The righteous are bold as a lion” — nothing behind to look for.
“We were bold in our God… after… shamefully entreated” — boldness surviving its cost.

pos: v. (to ask alms; rendering Greek epaiteo and prosaiteo)
etymology: Middle English beggen. Scripture treats begging as a real condition, an honest last resort, and once as something a steward could not face.
biblical_def: To beg is to ask alms. The unjust steward's calculation is famous: “I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed” (Luk 16:3). The blind man at Jericho sits by the way side begging (Mar 10:46), and the lame man at the Beautiful gate is laid daily to ask alms (Act 3:2). David records, “I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (Psa 37:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beg as to ask earnestly; to beseech; to entreat or supplicate with humility; and to ask alms or charity, to practice begging.
webster_full: BEG, v.t. To ask earnestly; to beseech; to entreat or supplicate with humility.
2. To ask or supplicate in charity.
3. To take for granted; to assume without proof.
BEG, v.i. To ask alms or charity; to practice begging; to live by asking alms.
scriptures: Luk 16:3
Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed.
And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sat by the highway side begging.
Act 3:2
And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple;
I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.
corruption_summary: Shame governs what help a person will accept, and Luke's steward preferred fraud to begging because of how it would look.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16:3 records an honest self-assessment leading to a dishonest plan: what shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. He was unfit for labour and unwilling to be seen asking, so he chose fraud. The sequence is worth noting because shame, not need, was the operative constraint. A great many bad decisions are made by people who could have asked for help and could not bear to.

Psalm 37:25 is a verse to be handled carefully. David reports his own long observation — I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. It is testimony rather than a universal guarantee, and Scripture elsewhere records righteous men in real destitution. What it does establish is a settled pattern in God's providence over a lifetime, offered by a man who had seen a great deal.
roots_summary: Greek epaiteo (G1871), to beg; prosaiteo (G4319), to ask persistently; ptochos (G4434), a crouching beggar.
roots_lines: Greek epaiteo (G1871) — to beg; only Luke 16:3.
Greek prosaiteo (G4319) — to beg persistently; Mark 10:46, John 9:8.
Greek eleemosune (G1654) — alms; Acts 3:2-3, to ask alms of them that entered.
usage: “I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed” — shame as the operative constraint.
“Blind Bartimaeus… sat by the highway side begging” — and would not be silenced.
“Nor his seed begging bread” — testimony from a long life.
